TMLM:UNAM	01000B5B	CheatTerminal_Attachments	1	-1	to_translate	The way this works, you need to be "holding" the item in your hands. Not having it equipped, but having the item dropped into the world, then physically pick it up. On PC, by default, holding E on the keyboard picks up an item on the ground. On XBOX, it is the A button on the controller. Once you are "holding" the item, you can verify it is in your hands by moving your view around, and if the object follows your view, it is in your hands. You will notice trying to pickup a weapon or piece of armor on the ground, holding the use key just equips it. Simply iron sighting into a weapon will allow you to pick up the item on the ground.\r\n\r\nThen from there, you simply select the attachments you want added to the item, and they will be attached. Some attachments can be stacked like the Armor's Damage Resistance. Some cannot, some will overwrite the attachment slots for others. Experimenting is encouraged. If you do not care about screwing up your save, you can stop reading now.\r\n\r\nHowever, do note: Try not to attach things to items that do not belong. Starfield has robust internal mechanisms to reject things that do not belong, like trying to attach weapon mods to armor. Some attachments are generic, like they go on all armors and while it may seem superficially working now, it may cause issues down the line, like it may say the weapon does 999999999999 damage, but then you shoot someone, and it ends up healing them because computers display numbers weirdly.\r\n\r\nWhile Starfield is a 64-bit game, and you'd think by now Bethesda has learned how to code properly, but I would not put it past them to still be treating things like damage and resistance as lower-tier integers like 32, 16 or even 8-bit signed integers, of which they have a 2147483647, 32767 and 128 limit respectively. Unsigned they would have 4294967295, 65535 and 255 limit respectively.\r\n\r\nThanks for coming to my TED talk.

TMLM:ITXT	01000050	CheatTerminal_NewGamePlus_VariantChance	13	-1	to_translate	What is this?
TMLM:UNAM	01000050	CheatTerminal_NewGamePlus_VariantChance	1	-1	to_translate	The Variant Chance setting controls how likely it is for a special variation of Constellation--by default, it's set to 15%. This means that, under normal conditions, there's a 15% chance that a quest variant will be triggered once the player has progressed far enough in the story. When the game reaches this point, it rolls a random number from 0 to 100. If that number is 15 or lower, a variant is allowed to play out. If the number is higher, the opportunity is lost entirely and the game proceeds with the standard quest--no variants will occur, even if forced. This roll is the gatekeeper that determines whether variety enters the picture or not.\r\n\r\n~Summation written by Microsoft Copilot.

TMLM:UNAM	01000052	CheatTerminal_NewGamePlus_Variant	1	-1	to_translate	In Starfield, entering New Game Plus (NG+) means stepping into an alternate universe, literally. Each time you pass through the Unity, you're reborn in a new version of the galaxy where the Lodge and its inhabitants may be wildly different. These universe variations are randomly selected and can range from subtle shifts to bizarre twists: you might meet a version of yourself, find Constellation replaced by children, or discover that Sarah Morgan is now a potted plant. Some universes are humorous, others dark, and a few even let you recruit your alternate self as a companion. While the core gameplay remains intact, these variations add a surreal, multiversal flavor to each NG+ run, making every return to the stars feel fresh and unpredictable.\r\n\r\n~Summation written by Microsoft Copilot.\r\n\r\nYou must have entered the Unity at least twice for these to occur.
